newsitem.title: MEXICO: Mexico's Nafin sees placing more convertible paper.
newsitem.headline: Mexico's Nafin sees placing more convertible paper.

text.p: Mexican development bank Nacional Financiera (Nafin) could place a convertible bond or a bond with stock warrants before the end of the year worth about $100 million to $200 million, said Carlos Mendoza Valencia, Nafin's finance director.
"It is possible that we will place a bond exchangeable for shares this year," he said in an interview. "It would be worth between $100 million and $200 million."

The development bank, Mexico's largest, has a five-year bond with warrants attached coming due in December this year, and other such deals outstanding. The shares come from Nafin's considerable portfolio.

"We want to continue with these instruments because they are ... attractive to a segment of investors interested in the upside that a share portfolio can have, but who need to have a coupon," Mendoza said.
The convertible bonds should also help Nafin lower its interest costs.
Mendoza said the development bank was leaning toward a bond convertible to a basket of shares, rather than one weighted to Mexico's key IPC stock index.

"A well-defined basket of shares is easier to cover than an index which is made up of a large number of shares. The index of the Mexican bolsa (stock exchange) is very complicated because every two months the index can be changed," Mendoza said.
Nafin's share portfolio is now worth almost $1 billion, and analysts say the portfolio includes stock in many solid Mexican companies.
"Our share portfolio is growing for two reasons: one is because of the growth of the stock market index, and the other because of accumulated trading profits," Mendoza said.
As well as allowing the bank to aim at a specific segment of the investing community, the convertible instruments have other advantages.

"It defers the sale of the shares. Instead of selling $100 or $200 million worth of shares in the market, which could have a strong negative impact, with this mechanism it defers the impact, diluting it with time," Mendoza said.
Nafin has been talking with various investment banks on managing the issue, he said.
